scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Para Para originated in Japan in the early 1980s, influenced by European Italo disco and Euro disco music and the Japanese Takenoko-zoku youth subculture dancing choreographed routines in Harajuku.
It developed in VIP club rooms and pedestrian plazas.
on_screen: Map: Japan · East Asia
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Para Para is performed at club events, dance lessons, and cultural conventions worldwide.
It serves as a social dance fostering community among fans of Eurobeat and Japanese pop culture.
The dance's synchronized routines create a shared experience, with lessons preserving and transmitting choreography.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Para Para is danced in synchronized groups performing choreographed upper body movements—primarily arms and hands—specific to each song's routine.
Dancers step side to side and move hips slightly, with minimal leg movement except for stepping in place or hopping.
The rhythm follows a four-on-the-floor beat typical of Eurobeat music.
Watch for Wangan style, Maniac routines, OriPara.
on_screen: Hero video — MISSING
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Groups dance in lines or clusters facing forward, maintaining spacing for arm movements

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Para Para is danced mainly to Eurobeat music, a fast-paced electronic genre derived from Italo disco and Euro disco, characterized by a four-on-the-floor rhythm and upbeat tempo.
Variants include TechPara danced to hyper techno and TraPara danced to trance music.
Listen for the synthesizers, electronic drums, bass synth, vocals.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 150 beats a minute.
Eurobeat tracks feature a driving four-on-the-floor beat with bright synthesizer melodies, rapid hi-hats, and catchy vocal hooks, creating a high-energy dance atmosphere.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Para Para is primarily danced in club settings in Japan, including notable venues like Twin Star, Velfarre, and Maharaja.
Club events often begin with less danceable music and increase in energy.
Dancers wear casual or club attire; no specific costume is mandated.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key choreographer groups include Shishō Gundan, known for Twinstar routines, with members like Gori-shishō (Keita Fukaya) and Arai-shishō (Takashi Arai).
T-RREX, formed by Twinstar, Rie, Richie, and Xenon members, choreographs for StarFire.
Variants of Para Para include TechPara, danced to hyper techno music with faster and more complex arm movements, and TraPara (or ToraPara), danced to trance music with slower, more subdued movements.
Para Para descends from Japanese club and street dance cultures of the 1980s, influenced by European Italo disco and Euro disco music.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Para Para is variant of TechPara: Danced to hyper techno music with faster arm movements.
Para Para is variant of TraPara: Danced to trance music with slower, more subdued movements.
Para Para is shares music of Bon Odori: Similar arm movement style and group formation, traditional Japanese festival dance.
